concept.name: Invalidation condition
concept.definition: The predefined price level, event, or condition at which the trade thesis is considered proven wrong and the position must be exited regardless of emotion. It is the logical core of a stop: the exit occurs because the reason for the trade is gone, not merely because pain is felt.
concept.intuition: Decide at entry what would prove you wrong; when it happens, the debate is over.
concept.mechanics: Set before entry from the structure of the thesis (below the breakout level, on failure of the catalyst, on time-stop expiry) and operationalized as a hard stop order or an enforced mental exit. Together with position size it fixes per-trade risk: risk = (entry - invalidation) x size.
concept.formula: Position size = (account risk per trade in currency) / |entry price - invalidation price|; e.g., risking $500 with entry 50 and invalidation 48 gives 250 shares.
concept.failure_modes: Invalidations set too tight are hit by noise; set from pain tolerance rather than structure, they are arbitrary. The most common failure is moving or ignoring the level after entry, converting a defined-risk trade into an open-ended one.
concept.misconceptions: Invalidation is a statement about the thesis, not about how much money one is willing to lose - the two coincide only by deliberate design. Re-entering later on a new signal is fully consistent with having honored the original invalidation.
concept.example: Long at 50 on a range breakout, thesis invalid below 48; price closes at 47.8 and the trader exits without negotiation, later re-entering only when a fresh setup forms.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
